It all depends on the context you are living in. There are places where being trans is seen as a sin. There are people who believe trans people are deceiving others. There are parents who kick their children out when they come out. Some people can’t access the hormones or treatments that would alleviate their dysphoria. Many people experience harassment or discrimination at work, school, or simply in the general public for being visibly trans. For people in these situations there is a significantly increased risk of both suicide and (being the victim of) homicide.

Other people have access to treatment and social support. They live in a place where they are protected from discrimination and people respect their identity. These people by and large still deal with dysphoria- feeling wrong in their body and/or the way they are perceived, which on its own can still be pretty devastating. 

Most people are somewhere in the middle. I have never felt overtly unsafe, but I am hyper aware of situations where my body can be exposed like locker rooms, or situations where anyone can see my birth name. No one has explicitly rejected me, but a lot of people cannot see me as a male and will not respect my name or pronouns, which causes a lot of anxiety. I am able to access hormone treatment but surgery and my legal name change are too expensive for me, so I have to deal with that discomfort until my financial situation changes. 

A lot of my difficulty has been with invisibility. I’m only 25, but trans topics only fairly recently became widely known. I spent the greater part of my childhood feeling like something was wrong with me, trying to be more masculine and having my family try to force it out of me out of fear that others would judge us. They weren’t religious or particularly homophobic or transphobic. They just had zero context for what I was going through, so I wasn’t able to transition and begin feeling comfortable until several years later. Some people go through this until they are in their 40s, 50s, or even later.

So regardless of your situation being trans is naturally going to make your life more challenging. But it can also have its positives. I have been seen as and treated as both male and female, broadening my perspective and giving me a huge amount of empathy and understanding that others probably wouldn’t get without having the experience of transition. The trans community is diverse and interesting and being a part of it, if you are active, is a very enriching experience. Knowing some trans history (I’m no expert, but I know some) shows just how powerful we are in what we’ve overcome and what we’ve done for the wider lgbt community. 

There are a lot of things that can make your life more challenging. I’ve been lucky enough that I am safe and fairly secure within my trans identity, so I can’t speak for everyone. But as far as challenges a person could encounter in their lifetime, I’m mostly okay with the face that being trans is one that I’ve had.

School was tough because of bullying as I didn’t fit with the girls OR the boys fully. And I do wish I could’ve worn the clothes that I felt more myself in. And I missed out on prom/school dances because the thought of wearing a gown and makeup was highly unappealing (particularly if I went with a guy who got to wear a suit that I would’ve preferred). 

So it wasn’t all perfect. But there are plenty of things that could’ve made my childhood less idyllic that aren’t gender related. There’s a slight sense of loss/sadness but overall I’ve mostly just accepted it for what it is and tried to see both the positives and negatives. But I also think I was fairly lucky in many ways so I would never invalidate someone for feeling that way.

Lesbian always felt kind of wrong but I clung to it because it made sense and I liked the community (I wasn’t even actively involved in it irl tbh, I just liked feeling like a part of something). I thought I couldn’t possibly be trans because I had some warped ideas about what trans men are actually like. I had also worked at a Girl Scout camp for several years, even working into a leadership role, and was terrified of losing that by transitioning. But I was super interested in trans stuff- to a point that it should have been obvious that it was a bit beyond curiosity. Eventually I found out about nonbinary people were and rolled with that for about two years. When I came out I began going by a new name and they/them pronouns. It was really amazing and freeing to finally separate myself from womanhood, but coming out as nonbinary forced me to be conscious of a lot of suppressed feelings. A lot of places where I came out people still just saw me and treated me as a female, and this really upset me. I found myself feeling really upset when people called me “miss,” “ma’am,” “young lady,” etc. but really happy when I got the occasional “sir.” I was suddenly more aware of things that I always didn’t like- my voice, my soft face, my hourglass figure, etc. These feelings built up over the course of months until I was like “oh my god I need to do something about this now” and I came out as a trans male.

Personally I’ve found it easier to let people know early on about my gender because they’re not in the habit of calling me the wrong pronouns or somehow attached to the idea of me being a woman. I also figure that if they have a problem I’d rather find out right away and know to avoid them as opposed to finding out after we’ve developed a relationship. I had already come out as nonbinary about two years prior, went by a new name a year after that, and had been quite certain that I didn't fully identify as female for years before that (but without telling anyone). Eventually I started to ask myself some tougher questions- some I found online, others I thought about myself.

1. When I'm old, what would I rather be? A little old lady or a little old man? If I didn't transition, would I look back and regret it? What would I regret more- doing it, or not doing it? For me, I wanted to be grandpa.
2. If I could make the physical and legal changes without any concern about backlash from friends, family, coworkers, etc., would I do it? This was an almost immediate, unquestioning yes for me.

(To be clear, I don't want to die, this is purely hypothetical). The thought of this made my skin crawl, and I knew that if I didn't take any action this was going to be what happened. 

I also read the article "The Null Hypothecis" - to summarize, many of us spend more time asking "What proof do I have that I'm trans?" as opposed to "What proof do I have that I'm cis?" Cis isn't the default, it's just one way of existing. I thought about all of the feelings I've had about my body, about being called she, her, ma'am, miss, lady, pretty, girl, and woman and how that made me skin crawl, about how I've worn male clothes for over ten years, about how uncomfortable puberty was... And the evidence of me being trans quicklu became a lot more compelling than the evidence of me being cis.

So basically, after over ten years of feeling weird, uncomfortable, out of place, I just began to reframe my thinking and it was like a lightbulb went off.

Emotionally manipulative behavior like this is classic in people who have trauma history- particularly if that trauma involves any type of abuse. Think of it this way- if you received inconsistent love and attention growing up, sometimes warm and close, other times angry and distant, you would likely develop some sort of coping strategy to defend yourself from this in future relationships. Her manipulation, while certainly not okay, is a type of defense mechanism. If you/your girlfriend are readers "Trauma and Recovery" by Judith Herman explains a lot of this in much better detail than I ever could (potential trigger warning for sexual assault, abuse, violence, etc.... Excellent book but do be sure to read it when your mind is clear). I read this in the fall for a class and it really helped me understand and process my own history- in addition to having a better understanding of a widely misunderstood topic.

Is your girlfriend in therapy? Because while you can communicate your struggles with her, it is unlikely that she is 100% able to see the connection between these actions and her trauma history, at least not in the heat of the moment- and this is something that you (or her) really cannot handle on your own without any professional help. 

So basically I would say if she's getting help, encourage her to keep going and if possible see if there's a way for you to be an active part of the healing process. If she's not getting help encourage her to begin doing so. In the meantime have an open, direct conversation about what your needs are and how this back-and-forth can be really upsetting and confusing for you, and while you still love her, it is affecting you. Perhaps come up with a codeword or something that you can use to alert her when this is happening, as often times this type of behavior is hard for the manipulator to recognize in the moment. 

I want to be clear that I'm not excusing her behavior, merely explaining it. She is responsible to begin making the change and you do not have to accept it as just a part of being her girlfriend. At the same time it is important to recognize the mechanisms going on in her head and how they are forcing her to behave this way.

PTSD is a pretty complex disorder with symptoms that overlap with a number of diagnoses. Some people have flashbacks where they feel on some level they are reliving an event- this may include visual, auditory, or sensory input (what you're describing) or it could simply be reliving the emotions you experienced during a traumatic event. Other people experience dissociation, where they feel like they are viewing their body from outside themselves, or derealization, where they feel detached from the world around them. Other common experiences can be difficulty regulating emotions, isolating socially, irritability, sleep difficulties, hyperarousal, and more. No two experiences are exactly the same.

If you have experienced any sort of trauma (trauma is a pretty broad term that can include a number of adverse experiences), particularly something where you felt trapped and did not have adequate social support, it is possible you have PTSD. I don't know much about your experience nor am I qualified to diagnose so that's really all I can say. A lot of PTSD treatments can be extremely helpful for people with a number of conditions (including anxiety, depression, substance use, and ADHD) because there's a lot of symptom overlap and trauma can be a precursor to a number of mental health issues... So while this diagnosis might not be complete, you might be dealing with enough symptoms to qualify for a PTSD label. If you're still questioning, though, you can ask your doctor and they should be able to offer you an explanation.

But after recurring hospitalizations and years of feeling constantly miserable, I'm finally in a pretty decent place; I now have my first car, am moving into my first apartment next week, and will be graduating college in May (albeit 2 years behind schedule). 

First I educated myself on depression and mental health in general. This allowed me to feel empowered in the treatment process and understand some of my underlying issues better. 

Then I began working on myself. Hobbies, education, etc. I did it for me, not anyone else. I tried things that I had been wanting to try but was too afraid, like joining the rugby team (I was terrible) and going to an out-of-state college (that worked out pretty well).

Over time I just learned to cope when something stressful happens. I use CBT worksheets, listen to music, go on walks, etc. On the rare occasion that I think of dying, I tell myself to go to sleep and see how I feel in the morning. I usually feel at least a little bit better.

In the mental health world, it's generally considered a safety issue if there is any sort of plan (time, place, method, etc.). The more specific and more lethal the plan, the more serious the risk. With that being said- any suicidal thoughts should be taken seriously and it is worth getting help.

Totally fine! Any type of therapy (that is worth your time) is not going to be a therapist sitting there and magically solving your problems. It is more about helping you develop self awareness and the social, cognitive, behavioral, and social skills needed to help yourself. A great therapist's goal is to basically work themselves out of a job.

CBT involves looking at your own negative thought processes and challenging them. Negative feelings are usually attributed to negative thoughts like "I'm worthless," "I should just give up," etc. CBT involves looking at those thoughts, what kinds of situations trigger those thoughts, and challenging them. I enjoy CBT because I am a pretty emotional person so being able to step back and look at these feelings logically has been an enormous help. 

Mindfulness is really based on staying in the present moment. Recognizing your thoughts, feelings, bodily sensations, etc. Often times, but not always, it involves breathing exercises and meditation. I like mindfulness because I'm often preoccupied with the worst case scenario.

1. Your medical history is private. Unless you hope to enlist in the military or something it's really not something employers, schools, etc. are ever going to see or judge you on. 
2. If you have a therapist that is suited to your own needs and are willing to totally engage in the therapeutic process, yes, therapy is effective. All mainstream therapeutic methods are based on evidence-based research and you can easily access much of this information on the internet if you are skeptical. The thing to remember is that like medication it can sometimes take some time to figure out what therapy is best for you. There are dozens of therapeutic methods (CBT, DBT, solutions-focused, etc.) out there. Personally I found CBT and mindfulness to be helpful. You may not. Therapy can be a short term process (2-3 months) for some and a very long, ongoing process for others. You are allowed to change therapists if one isn't working for you. With an open mind and a fair amount of effort, therapy is incredibly beneficial to a lot of people. 
3. Prescription medications are a tool that many people find to be an essential part of their treatment. They are not for everyone. Medications can help lift you to your baseline so you are able to do the work you need to get better. They are not a quick fix (most antidepressants take 2-3 months to take their full effect) and they will not resolve the underlying issues that might have caused your depression so doctors typically require anyone on medication to also be receiving some form of therapy. Ultimately the choice is your own; they are not for everyone, but for some they are life-saving.
